analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal funds from enforcing an executive order barring contractors from hiring permanent striker replacements.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited the use of any fiscal year 1995 appropriated money to issue, implement, or enforce an executive order or rule that limits the ability of federal contractors, subcontractors, or vendors to hire permanent replacements for employees who are lawfully on strike. It was written to block the Clinton administration's 1995 executive order restricting federal contractors from permanently replacing striking workers. The bill was sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal contractors and employers generally, who would keep the power to hire permanent replacements for striking workers and would not have to comply with the executive order the bill targeted. Under longstanding labor law, hiring permanent replacements removes the striker's job, so the bill would have strengthened employers' hand in any strike at a federal contractor.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar any fiscal year 1995 appropriated funds from being used to issue, implement, administer, or enforce any executive order, rule, or regulation that limits a federal contractor's ability to hire permanent replacements for lawfully striking employees.

It would have defunded the executive branch's effort to make federal contract work contingent on employers not permanently replacing strikers, leaving contractors free to staff struck workplaces with new permanent hires.

The bill's stated purpose was that Congress, not the executive branch, should decide national labor-management policy, arguing the White House should not use the federal procurement process to make major changes in labor relations.

analysis.who_pays: Workers on strike at federal contractor workplaces. Their main leverage is the threat to halt production, and the ability to hire permanent replacements erases that threat because a permanent replacement takes the striker's job for good. The bill would have preserved that employer power by starving the executive order of funds.

drawbacks.text: The bill's effect would fall on strikers: permanent replacement is the most severe lawful penalty for striking, since the replacement keeps the job after the dispute ends, and the bill would ensure federal money could not be used to enforce any limit on that practice.

A fair objection from supporters is that major national labor policy was being set by executive order through the procurement process rather than by legislation, and the bill's findings say Congress should decide labor-management policy as the representative body of the people.

The bill reaches only federal contractors and only fiscal year 1995 funds, so it would not have changed the underlying law on permanent replacements for the private sector generally — a narrow remedy that mainly benefits a specific set of employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to employers in the form of preserved bargaining leverage; the costs fall on workers whose right to strike is hollowed out when permanent replacements are available. The separation-of-powers argument raised in the bill's findings is a genuine debate, but the practical result of the bill would have been to weaken workers at federal contractor firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Labor Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Nancy Kassebaum, joined by original cosponsors including Sens. Coats, Gorton, and Hatch, introduced the bill on June 29, 1995; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
Six Republican senators signed on as cosponsors in total.
The action history shows no activity after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, for the rest of the 104th Congress, which ended January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the executive order it targeted was never defunded by Congress, so the employer-side change was blocked for the remainder of the Congress. Striking workers and their unions came out ahead relative to what the bill would have done; the broader dispute over the underlying executive order was left to the courts rather than settled by this legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Striking workers; the employer-backed bill died

for.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-KS), sponsor; chaired the committee the bill was referred to
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was then referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee she chaired; no further action was taken on it.

for.name: Sens. Dan Coats, Slade Gorton, and Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Joined Kassebaum as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; no action appears after the referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: His 1995 executive order barring federal contractors from hiring permanent replacements for striking workers was the policy the bill was written to defund; the administration maintained the order.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached the floor, so how the parties would have split on a vote was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would preserve their ability to permanently replace striking employees, removing the biggest threat a strike poses to an employer. The cost falls on the striking workers themselves.

industries.industry: Organized labor and workers at federal contractor workplaces
industries.note: Under the bill, federal money could not be used to enforce any limit on permanent replacements, weakening the leverage of strikers at federal contractor firms.
